GHSA-PFWX-36V6-832X.fc444066c05011ac993104782328b63f7ea48616:
test(update-interactive): isolate install cache per test to fix Windows flake (#33964)

`test/cli/update_interactive_install.test.ts` has been flaking on
Windows lanes (2019 x64, 2019 x64-baseline, 11 aarch64) since it was
introduced in #24280. In the 71700-71800 build range alone it shows up
in ~35 builds, usually passing on retry but occasionally going fully red
(e.g. build 71752, build 71675).

## Repro

On Windows with a cold cache, the unfixed file fails ~30% of the time:

```
Original test failures: 9 / 30
```

The captured stderr is:

```
ENOENT: failed opening cache/package/version dir for package is-number
```

## Cause

The two tests in the describe block run concurrently
(`describe.concurrent`) and both transitively depend on `is-number` (via
`is-even` -> `is-odd` -> `is-number` and `is-odd` -> `is-number`). Both
spawned `bun install` processes share the default global install cache,
and on Windows one of them hits ENOENT when the other is mid-write to
the same cache entry.

The original test also asserted the install exit code without draining
stdout/stderr, so CI only ever showed `Expected: 0 / Received: 1` with
no diagnostic.

## Fix

Give each test its own `BUN_INSTALL_CACHE_DIR` inside its temp dir. This
is the same pattern used across `test/cli/install/` (e.g.
`bun-run-dir.test.ts`, `GHSA-pfwx-36v6-832x.test.ts`,
`isolated-install.test.ts`). Also drain and surface stdout/stderr on the
initial install so a future failure reports the actual error.

## Verification

On Windows, 50 cold-cache iterations with the fix:

```
Fixed test failures: 0 / 50
```

Linux.

This is a test-only change; no `src/` behaviour is modified.

GHSA-PFWX-36V6-832X.f5d98191b7c0a605a4ee79c5e37a2933046728be:
fix(install): store and verify SHA-512 integrity hash for GitHub tarball dependencies (#27019)

## Summary

- Compute SHA-512 hash of GitHub tarball bytes during extraction and
store in `bun.lock`
- Verify the hash on subsequent installs when re-downloading, rejecting
tampered tarballs
- Automatically upgrade old lockfiles without integrity by computing and
persisting the hash
- Maintain backward compatibility with old lockfile format (no integrity
field)

Fixes GHSA-pfwx-36v6-832x

## Lockfile format change

```
Before: ["pkg@github:user/repo#ref", {}, "resolved-commit"]
After:  ["pkg@github:user/repo#ref", {}, "resolved-commit", "sha512-..."]
```

The integrity field is optional for backward compatibility. Old
lockfiles are automatically upgraded when the tarball is re-downloaded.

## Test plan

- [x] Fresh install stores SHA-512 integrity hash in lockfile
- [x] Re-install with matching hash succeeds
- [x] Re-install with mismatched hash rejects the tarball
- [x] Old lockfile without integrity is auto-upgraded with hash on
re-download
- [x] Cache hits still work without re-downloading
- [x] Existing GitHub dependency tests pass (10/10)
- [x] Existing git resolution snapshot test passes
- [x] Yarn migration snapshot tests pass

CVE-2023-44487.fa146573992c955986924043265bbbd92402afbf:
node:http2: rate-limit stream resets per connection (CVE-2023-44487, CVE-2025-8671)

A client that opens streams and immediately kills them could drive unbounded
work on a node:http2 server: the 'stream' handler ran and a response was
serialized for every cancelled stream, and the server never sent GOAWAY.

Port nghttp2's stream_reset_ratelim into the h2 engine: a token bucket of
1000 refilling at 33/s, charged per inbound RST_STREAM on server sessions
until this side has sent a GOAWAY, configurable through node's
streamResetBurst / streamResetRate (applied only when both are given,
floored to 1, like util.js updateOptionsBuffer + node_http2.cc). Resets the
engine itself sends in reaction to inbound frames (the MadeYouReset shape)
drain a second fixed bucket so the node options keep node's meaning. An
empty bucket tears the session down between frames with
GOAWAY(ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM) / NGHTTP2_ERR_FLOODED, surfaced as
ERR_HTTP2_ERROR; nghttp2 uses INTERNAL_ERROR, ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM matches the
engine's existing flood guard.
CVE-2023-44487.13805dd3b0bd92aea64ce18777b3c3b5c200497e:
h2: Rapid Reset cap, MAX_HEADER_LIST on initial HEADERS, §8.2.1 comment accuracy

- handleRstStream: bound cumulative client resets per connection at 1000
  (CVE-2023-44487); a HEADERS->RST flood keeps the concurrent-stream count
  near zero so MAX_STREAMS never trips. GOAWAY(ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM) past the
  cap, matching nginx/Go/nghttp2. Adds a regression that packs 1200
  HEADERS+RST pairs and asserts the GOAWAY code.
- handleHeaders: enforce MAX_HEADER_LIST on the initial HEADERS fragment
  before headerBlock.assign(), mirroring the check handleContinuation
  already runs on the same accumulator so a single large-frame block and
  a split block are bounded the same way.
- decodeHeaderBlock comment: describe what the name loop actually checks
  (the §8.2.1 MUST-level byte ranges) and note the tchar delimiter set as
  a deferred SHOULD alongside the existing §8.2.2/§8.3.1 gaps.
CVE-2023-44487.4fd91fb70f81c6d9705c931acf9e651151c6bca4:
http2: rate-limit rapid reset with a token bucket, make the concurrency check O(1)

The rapid-reset guard was a net-outstanding gauge: +1 per inbound peer
RST_STREAM, -1 per odd-id close_stream. The canonical CVE-2023-44487 flood
(HEADERS then RST_STREAM, holding nothing open) nets to zero across read
batches and never trips, and the refund fired for every odd-id close, so one
completed request per batch kept the counter pinned near zero.

Replace it with nghttp2's stream_reset_rate_limit model: a token bucket of
streamResetBurst tokens regenerated at streamResetRate per second on a
monotonic clock, drained once per inbound RST_STREAM on a known stream.
Running dry answers GOAWAY(ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM). close_stream no longer
touches the budget. streamResetRate is read from the session options next to
streamResetBurst; both default to nghttp2's values (1000 and 33).

The SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS check no longer rescans the stream map on
every HEADERS: peer_active_count is maintained incrementally by routing every
stream state write, insert, and removal through set_stream_state,
insert_stream, and remove_stream. The check now applies to both roles (a push
response promoting a reserved-remote stream counts against the client's
advertised limit), and inbound PUSH_PROMISE reservations, which section 5.1.2
exempts from that limit, are capped at nghttp2's
max_incoming_reserved_streams (200) and answered with
RST_STREAM(REFUSED_STREAM) past it.

The peer_resets_are_refunded_by_close_stream unit test asserted the broken
refund (32 HEADERS/RST batches, no GOAWAY); it is replaced by tests that pace
HEADERS then RST across read batches with a completed legitimate request
between each and assert the GOAWAY, plus tests for the timed refill, the
incremental gauge, the reserved-stream cap, and the client-side limit. The
paced scenario is also covered at the wire level in h2-conformance.test.ts,
where it fails against the previous design.
CVE-2023-44487.52fdb1f68a306099f654b250ebf60a9163691d85:
http2: enforce max_concurrent_streams and bound rapid-reset in the engine

The h2 connection engine inserted a Stream entry and dispatched
on_stream_open for every inbound HEADERS without checking the
advertised SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS (RFC 9113 5.1.2), and
inbound RST_STREAM was uncounted, so a HEADERS-then-RST flood
(CVE-2023-44487 shape) churned native and JS per-stream state
without bound.

handle_headers now refuses an over-cap new stream with
RST_STREAM(REFUSED_STREAM) before inserting any map entry or
firing on_stream_open; the header block is still HPACK-decoded
for table sync (4.3), last_stream_id advances so a follow-up
RST on the refused id is tolerated, and the refusal routes
through on_stream_rejected so maxSessionRejectedStreams budgets
the flood. handle_rst_stream counts server-side peer resets
against the invalid-frame budget (maxSessionInvalidFrames,
default 1000) so a rapid-reset flood that stays under the
concurrency cap still tears the session down.

CVE-2024-28182.a4971c6d09b34aa7446eb7d9f0e0ff8c685bb625:
node:http2: cap CONTINUATION frames per header block (CVE-2024-28182)

The inbound engine bounded a header block under reassembly only by its
byte size, so a peer sending HEADERS without END_HEADERS followed by
zero-length CONTINUATION frames could hold the session in header-block
state indefinitely: nothing ever errored, the request stayed pending, and
the receiver spent a core parsing 9-byte frames. This is the bug nghttp2
fixed as CVE-2024-28182; node errors after the 8th CONTINUATION.

Count CONTINUATION frames on the in-flight block record and fail the
connection once a block exceeds nghttp2's NGHTTP2_DEFAULT_MAX_CONTINUATIONS
(8), the same way node does: GOAWAY(INTERNAL_ERROR) on the wire and an
NghttpError with errno -905 ("Too many CONTINUATION frames following a
HEADER frame") on the session. The counter lives on HeaderBlockInFlight,
so every HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE that opens a block starts from zero and
the budget is per block, not per session. Applies to clients and servers
alike since they share the engine.

Tests pin the exact boundary on both sides (8 accepted, the 9th rejected
even when it carries END_HEADERS), the per-block reset (response and
trailers each using the full budget on one stream), the PUSH_PROMISE
opener, and the GOAWAY error code a server emits.
CVE-2024-28182.a5c86aec746ce69fb480d37a455640d4fd2cc475:
fetch(h2): cap CONTINUATION frames per header block (CVE-2024-28182) (#36411)

### Problem
- A hostile HTTP/2 origin can pin a `fetch()` forever: it answers with
`HEADERS` without `END_HEADERS`, then streams zero-length `CONTINUATION`
frames. The promise never settles and the client burns CPU parsing
9-byte frame headers (CVE-2024-28182 class; the `node:http2` side is
#36410).
- `src/http/h2_client/dispatch.rs`, `FT_CONTINUATION` arm: the only
bound on a header block is `LOCAL_MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE` on accumulated
bytes. An empty payload never advances that, so nothing ends the
sequence.

### Fix
- Add `continuation_count: u8` to `ClientSession`, zeroed at the top of
the `FT_HEADERS` arm and incremented in `FT_CONTINUATION`; past
`LOCAL_MAX_CONTINUATIONS` (8) the connection fails with
`HTTP2EnhanceYourCalm`, which `error_code_for` already maps to
`ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM` on the GOAWAY.
- The value and behaviour match nghttp2
(`NGHTTP2_DEFAULT_MAX_CONTINUATIONS`) and node 22: 8 frames accepted,
the 9th rejected even when it carries `END_HEADERS`.
- One reset at the top of `FT_HEADERS` is sufficient because
`dispatch_frame` already rejects any non-`CONTINUATION` frame while a
block is open, so every `HEADERS` that reaches the arm starts a new
block; this covers the tracked-stream and orphan (already-RST'd stream)
branches alike.
- 8 x 16 KiB (default `MAX_FRAME_SIZE`) is 128 KiB of compressed
headers, below the existing 256 KiB byte cap, so the pre-existing
`CONTINUATION flood is bounded` test now sees `HTTP2EnhanceYourCalm`;
its assertion is updated.
- Verified in `test/js/web/fetch/fetch-http2-adversarial.test.ts` (20/20
with the fix; 3 fail on the released binary):
- `zero-length CONTINUATION flood is rejected`: the repro, times out
without the fix.
- `header block split across the full CONTINUATION budget is accepted`:
8 frames deliver a 200.
- `9th CONTINUATION is rejected even if it ends the block`: pins the cap
at exactly 8 and the comparison at `>`.
- `CONTINUATION budget resets for each header block on a stream`: a 103
block and the final 200 block on one stream each use all 8 frames; fails
with the reset removed (checked by removing it and rebuilding).
- `fetch-http2-client.test.ts` still 62/62.

### Background
- An HTTP/2 header block starts in a `HEADERS` frame and, when
`END_HEADERS` is not set, continues in `CONTINUATION` frames on the same
stream; until one arrives with `END_HEADERS`, no other frame is allowed
on the connection (RFC 9113 4.3, 6.10). A response may carry several
blocks on one stream: 1xx informational blocks, the final response, and
trailers.
- HPACK state is connection-wide, so the fetch client also assembles and
decodes blocks for streams it has already reset (the "orphan" path in
`dispatch.rs`) to keep the decoder in sync; the cap has to apply there
too.
- `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM` is the HTTP/2 error code for "peer is generating
excessive load"; `HTTP2EnhanceYourCalm` is the `fetch()` error the
client already uses for its other flood limits.

CVE-2024-36139.c0caf8a6949e58146e6dfcf4c8de1c93b54f50a1:
Rewrite node:path natively on JSString storage; match Node.js v26 exactly

node:path is now a line-for-line port of Node's lib/path.js in Path.cpp that
reads each argument's Latin-1 or UTF-16 backing store directly instead of
converting every input to UTF-8 and every result back.

- Results that are slices of an input (basename, dirname, extname, parse) are
  returned as substrings sharing the input's buffer; results that must be
  assembled (join, resolve, normalize, relative) are built once in a stack
  buffer of the inputs' width, and an unchanged input is returned as-is.
- isAbsolute, posix toNamespacedPath and format live in path.ts, where the JIT
  can inline them; the .bind() wrappers around every export are gone.
- Behaviour now matches Node.js v26.3.0: Windows reserved device names
  (CON/COM1/...) in normalize and join, the CVE-2024-36139 traversal fixes,
  \\.\ and \\?\ device roots in resolve/toNamespacedPath, Unicode-aware
  case folding in win32.relative, Node's argument names and error messages,
  and Node's property order and function names on the module object. The
  upstream test-path-*.js files are re-synced verbatim; the one remaining
  deviation (path.resolve does not call a monkey-patched process.cwd) keeps
  its explanatory comment.
- test/js/node/path/node-path-parity.test.ts checks 1540 generated inputs
  against outputs recorded from Node, plus long inputs and many-argument calls.
- bench/snippets/path.mjs covers every function on posix and win32 with
  Latin-1, UTF-16 and 2000-character inputs. On an M-series Mac the geometric
  mean is 3.5x faster than the previous implementation (no case slower than
  1.27x) and 2.2x faster than Node.

The old Rust implementation (src/runtime/node/path.rs), its per-VM scratch
buffers in rare_data, and the Bun__Path__* / Bun__Node__Path_joinWTF exports
are removed; the two C++ callers use Bun::NodePath::dirname/join directly.

node:path: port Node's drive and reserved device name guards to win32 normalize and join

path.win32.normalize now prefixes a relative result with .\ when it would
otherwise look like a drive (c:) or end a segment with a colon (CON:), and
recognizes reserved DOS device names (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9, LPT1-9 and
superscript variants) as device roots. path.win32.join skips normalization
when a joined part is a reserved device name, leaving .. segments
uncollapsed. This matches Node's behavior since the CVE-2024-36139 fix.

Fixes #35610
CVE-2024-36139.4da3f3bb53a042be1331b360aee87554f8d94f86:
path: port Node v26 win32 device-root and reserved-name handling

path.win32 was still on the Node v21.6.1 algorithm and was missing three
upstream changes.

Device roots. \\.\X and \\?\X are device roots, not UNC shares, so
resolve() and normalize() must not append a trailing separator:
path.win32.resolve('\\\\?\\foo') returned '\\\\?\\foo\\'
where Node returns '\\\\?\\foo'. toNamespacedPath inherited the same
extra separator through resolve.

CVE-2024-36139. path.win32.normalize('test/../C:/Windows') returned
'C:\\Windows' - a relative path normalizing into a different drive root.
Node returns '.\\C:\\Windows'. normalize now applies the same guard: when
the input is relative, has no device, and contains a colon, the result is
prefixed with '.\\'.

Reserved device names. CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9 and LPT1-9 (including the
superscript COM\u00b9 spellings) are recognised in normalize's root match and
in join, which skips normalization entirely when any joined segment is a
reserved name so that '..' after 'CON:' is not resolved away.

Restores four upstream tests to verbatim v26.3.0: test-path-normalize,
test-path-makelong, test-path-join, test-url-urltooptions.

urlToHttpOptions now rejects non-objects with ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE, matching
Node's validateObject(url, 'url', kValidateObjectAllowObjects).

The Bun-owned to-namespaced-path test asserted the old trailing separator;
its two expectations now match real Node output.
CVE-2024-36139.ed1812b7f017f4860ebd1a6434f24e48cc83ad83:
path: normalize reserved Windows device names; domain: node's thrown-error ordering

path.win32.normalize() did not know about reserved DOS device names, so
`CON:` came back as `CON:` instead of `.\CON:.`, and a relative path with a
colon such as `foo:/bar` was not made explicitly relative (CVE-2024-36139).

`\\?\` device roots are recognized (including `\\?\COM1:`), and both the
reserved and colon cases prefix the result with `.\`. The reserved-name list
covers the superscript COM¹/²/³ and LPT¹/²/³ spellings in both the UTF-8 and

domain was still active. Node exits the domain first and clears the stack
afterwards, so `process.domain` is undefined inside the handler and null once
the tick ends.

CVE-2021-22939.c3fcd1ad4a60e6ee3092fb804f2f59cc1075dc40:
node:tls: only an explicit false for rejectUnauthorized disables verification

Node's CVE-2021-22939 fix checks `rejectUnauthorized !== false`: every
other value, including null, keeps certificate verification on. Bun's
client connect paths stored the raw option value and then checked it
for truthiness, so rejectUnauthorized: null silently bypassed
verification where Node rejects. Normalize to a real boolean at each
store site (the TLSSocket constructor, Server setSecureContext, and
the three Socket.prototype.connect TLS paths). The bindgen layer
already rejects 0/""/1 with ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE, so null was the
only non-boolean that reached these sites.

Also: declare `session` with let before the try in the resumption
test instead of hoisting with var.

CVE-2021-23222.9a4d8ab835fe65ea013745e9c5c8233f16ed085d:
Bun.SQL(postgres): send plaintext startup when sslmode=prefer and server declines TLS

When the server answers the SSLRequest with 'N', the prefer branch only
set TlsStatus::SslNotAvailable and looped back, never writing a
StartupMessage. The connection then idled until connectionTimeout. This
meant any non-SSL Postgres (the docker default) was unreachable via a
standard libpq ?sslmode=prefer URL.

Call start() to send the plaintext StartupMessage on the same socket
and return Ok(()) so any bytes that arrive alongside the 'N' are
discarded rather than dispatched (the libpq CVE-2021-23222 shape).

Update the tls_ctx leak test's mock server to answer the
StartupMessage in a second round trip instead of packing AuthOk after
'N' in one write, which depended on the old continue behaviour.

CVE-2024-27980.2c21d71ae746e16d465a7171a7595b9eec88132c:
debug-adapter: pass shell:true when resolved path is a batch file

The previous commit resolved bare command names via PATH/PATHEXT but
still spawned the resolved path directly. That fixes the bare-name
lookup but not the CVE-2024-27980 hardening: Node's ProcessWrap::Spawn
rejects any options.file ending in .bat/.cmd with EINVAL regardless of
whether the path is absolute. The check is suffix-based — see
node:src/util-inl.h IsWindowsBatchFile.

For the reported npm-wrapper scenario — where bun.cmd is the only
discoverable entry on PATH — the resolved path is C:\...\bun.cmd and
spawn still fails.

Change resolveCommand to return { command, useShell } and have the
adapter pass shell: useShell to spawn. With shell:true Node rewrites
the file to cmd.exe and wraps the invocation as /d /s /c "...", so
the batch-file check in the C++ layer sees cmd.exe and succeeds.

Expanded the regression test to assert useShell is set correctly for
bare names, absolute paths, and reversed PATHEXT orderings.
CVE-2024-27980.dafbb6b7f0003f76f568cac1fc0319766bf8bac6:
debug-adapter: resolve command via PATH/PATHEXT on Windows

child_process.spawn on Windows does not apply PATHEXT resolution, and
post-CVE-2024-27980 it refuses to launch .cmd/.bat files unless shell:
true is set. Bun installed via the npm wrapper on Windows lands on PATH
as bun.cmd, so the debug adapter's default spawn("bun", ...) call fails
with EINVAL.

Resolve bare command names to an absolute .exe/.cmd path before
spawning. Avoids the shell: true escaping surface and keeps ENOENT
error messages intact when the command is genuinely missing.

Fixes #29636

| | macOS (ImageIO + vImage) | Windows (WIC) | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|
| JPEG/PNG/WebP | static codecs (output identical across platforms) |
static codecs | static |
| GIF/BMP | static `codec_gif.zig`/`codec_bmp.zig` | static | static |

wrapped in an explicit autoreleasepool per WorkPool call. WIC encode
threads `ImageQuality`/`HeifCompressionMethod` through a C++ shim so the
SDK's own VARIANT layout is authoritative. Symbol resolution stays lazy
(dlsym/CoCreateInstance), zero startup cost.

GHSA-JFHR-4V9P-9RM4.ede635b8a921e95f0d847641a48e4d448baf9a7f:
fix(install): store tarball integrity hash in lockfile for HTTPS dependencies (#27018)

## Summary
- HTTPS/URL tarball dependencies were not having their integrity hash
stored in the lockfile, allowing a malicious server to change the
tarball contents without detection on subsequent installs
- Now computes a sha512 hash from the downloaded tarball bytes during
extraction and stores it in both the binary lockfile and text bun.lock
- The hash is verified on re-download, matching the behavior of npm
registry packages
- Old lockfiles without integrity hashes continue to work (backward
compatible)

## Changes
- `src/install/integrity.zig`: Added `Integrity.forBytes()` to compute
sha512 from raw bytes
- `src/install/install.zig`: Added `integrity` field to `ExtractData`
struct
- `src/install/PackageManagerTask.zig`: Compute hash from tarball bytes
for both remote and local tarball tasks
- `src/install/PackageManager/processDependencyList.zig`: Set
`package.meta.integrity` from computed hash
- `src/install/lockfile/bun.lock.zig`: Serialize/deserialize integrity
for `remote_tarball` and `local_tarball` types

## Test plan
- [x] Integrity hash is stored in text lockfile for tarball URL deps
- [x] Integrity hash is consistent/deterministic across reinstalls
- [x] Integrity mismatch (changed tarball content) causes install
failure
- [x] Old lockfiles without integrity still install successfully
(backward compat)
- [x] Fresh installs produce integrity hashes
- [x] All 12 existing tarball tests pass (no regressions)
- [x] Tests fail with `USE_SYSTEM_BUN=1` (confirms fix is effective)

CVE-2018-7160.7f57c9c74733f39da5557c6bf73edee4634e87d7:
fix(debugger): use crypto.randomUUID() for WebSocket auth token

Replace Math.random().toString(36) with crypto.randomUUID() for generating
the debugger WebSocket path token. Math.random() is not cryptographically
secure and produces predictable output, making it possible for local
attackers to guess the token and connect to the debugger via Chrome DevTools
Protocol. This is the same class of vulnerability as Node.js CVE-2018-7160.
